opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The basic intuition is that a single language model, when it answers a question in one pass, often makes mistakes it could actually catch if it were prompted to look again. In our work on multi-agent debate, we found that if you take several instances of a model, have each one propose an answer and its reasoning, and then let them read each other's responses and revise over a few rounds, they tend to converge on answers that are noticeably more accurate and more factually grounded than any single instance would produce alone.

So why does that matter for training data? Right now, a lot of improvement in these models comes from having high-quality data, and the best data has traditionally come from people, which is expensive and hard to scale. Debate gives you a way to have the model generate data that's better than what it would produce on its own. The agents act as critics for one another: one model might make an arithmetic slip or hallucinate a fact, and another will point it out, and through that back-and-forth, errors get filtered out. You essentially get a form of self-consistency and verification without needing an external labeler.

Once you have those refined, debated outputs, you can use them to fine-tune the model, and then repeat the process. That gives you a kind of self-improvement loop where the model is learning from a stronger version of itself, the "society" of agents, rather than just from its own first guesses. One thing we found is that if you fine-tune a single model on its own outputs repeatedly, you tend to get collapse; the responses become less diverse and performance plateaus. But if you maintain multiple agents, and even specialize them into different roles, like generators and critics, trained on different slices of the debate data, you preserve diversity of reasoning, and the improvements keep going across more rounds.

More broadly, I think it reflects something about how intelligence works in people too. We rarely get things right in isolation; we reason better when we argue, check each other's work, and compose different perspectives. Multi-agent debate is a way of building that into how models generate and learn from data.

r001.rationale: The response says debated model instances converge on answers that are more accurate than any single instance would produce alone.

r002.rationale: It says refined answers from debate can be used to fine-tune the model, then the process can be repeated.

r003.rationale: It describes a structured process of proposing answers, reviewing other agents’ responses, and revising over rounds, and says this back-and-forth supports better reasoning.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So the way I think about it is that a lot of the data we train language models on today is essentially one-shot. You ask a model a question, it gives an answer, and that answer, whether it's right or wrong, becomes part of what the next model learns from. And the problem is that any single model, on any single pass, is going to make mistakes. It'll hallucinate a fact, it'll drop a step in a math problem, it'll be confidently wrong.

What multi-agent debate does is it takes that same question and gives it to several instances of a model, or several different models, and lets each of them produce an answer independently. Then you show each agent what the others said and ask it to reconsider. And you iterate that a few rounds. What we found, somewhat to our surprise, is that this process tends to converge on answers that are substantially more accurate than what any single model produces on its own. The models actually catch each other's errors. If one model makes an arithmetic slip, another one will often notice it, and the first one will update.

So why does that matter for training data? Well, if you can take a set of questions and run them through debate, you end up with a set of answers that are higher quality than what you started with. And now you can train on that. You're using the models themselves to generate a cleaner, more consistent dataset than you'd get from just sampling them once. And the nice thing is that it's fairly general. It's not a trick that only works on math. We saw gains on factual questions, on reasoning tasks, on things like biographies where the base models would just make things up.

There's also a kind of self-improvement angle here that I find really interesting. You train on the debate outputs, you get a slightly better model, you run debate again with that model, and the outputs get better still. So it's a loop. And I think a lot of the exciting direction in the field is figuring out how far you can push loops like that without having to go collect more human-labeled data every time.

r001.rationale: It says debate tends to produce answers substantially more accurate than a single model’s answer and describes agents catching one another’s errors.

r002.rationale: It explicitly describes training on the higher-quality answers generated through debate, then repeating the process with the improved model.

r003.rationale: The response describes debate rounds and reconsideration, but does not state that imposing structure on generation encourages additional reasoning.

astra-6.text:
One challenge with training on model-generated data is that a model can produce an answer that sounds convincing but is wrong. If you train directly on that output, you can reinforce the same mistakes.

With multi-agent debate, you have several models independently propose answers, then examine and critique one another’s reasoning. One model might catch an error that another missed, and that feedback gives them a chance to revise their answers. So you can potentially get a better training example out of the interaction than you would from a single response.

The models don’t necessarily have to be different—you can get different perspectives from separate instances of the same model. Agreement alone doesn’t guarantee correctness, because they can share the same blind spots. But debate gives you a way to scrutinize generated answers before using them as training data.

r001.rationale: It explains that debate can catch errors and let models revise, potentially producing a better training example than a single response.

r002.rationale: It describes using the improved answers from the debate interaction as training data.

r003.rationale: It describes critique and revision through debate, but does not say that imposing structure on generation encourages additional reasoning.

sol-6.1.text:
One challenge with generating training data from a language model is that the model can produce an answer that sounds convincing but is actually wrong. If you train on that directly, you can reinforce those mistakes.

With multi-agent debate, you have several models propose answers independently, then look at one another’s reasoning and revise their responses. That creates an opportunity to catch errors that a single model might miss. A model might notice a faulty assumption or point out a contradiction, and the others can use that feedback to improve their answers.

So you’re using additional computation to produce potentially better training examples, without needing a human to write every answer. Of course, agreement doesn’t guarantee correctness—the models can share the same mistakes. But debate gives you a way to critique and refine generated data before using it for training.

r001.rationale: It says debate can catch errors a single model might miss and help the models improve their answers, making potentially better examples than the initial answers.

r002.rationale: It describes models revising answers through debate and says the refined generated data can then be used for training.

r003.rationale: It describes a debate and revision process, but does not state that imposing structure on generation encourages additional reasoning.
